items.prompt: Which description defines a pure function?

options.label: It never takes any arguments and returns a constant
Same inputs always give the same output, with no side effects
It is declared with the keyword pure and cannot call other functions
It only works on numbers and returns numbers

rubric: A pure function is deterministic and has no side effects.
Distractors confuse purity with argument types or syntax.

items.prompt: What does immutable data mean?

options.label: Data that is stored only in a file on disk
Data that is changed automatically by the compiler
Data that cannot be changed after it is created
Data that can only be read by one function

rubric: Immutable values cannot be modified once created.
Distractors mix immutability with storage or access.

items.prompt: What is a higher-order function?

options.label: A function that uses more memory than others
A function that is declared at the top of a file
A function that takes or returns another function
A function that always runs before all of the other functions

rubric: Higher-order functions accept or return functions.
Distractors rely on ordering, memory or placement.

items.prompt: Which operation is the standard name for keeping only the items that pass a test?

options.label: map
reduce
zip
filter

rubric: filter keeps items for which a predicate is true.
map transforms, reduce combines.

items.prompt: What is a closure?

options.label: A block that closes a file or connection after use
A function bundled with the variables from where it was defined
A function that runs once and then cannot be called again
A pure function that is sealed so it cannot read outside values

rubric: A closure captures variables from its defining scope.
Distractors rely on the everyday meaning of 'close'.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common examples of side effects? Select all that apply.

options.label: Modifying a global variable
Returning the sum of two arguments
Writing to a file
Creating a new local variable inside the function body

items.prompt: A teammate says, "We will write `compose(f, g)` so that we chain small functions into one new function." You are asked which core FP idea this describes.

options.label: Memory allocation
Method inheritance
Polymorphism
Composition

rubric: Composition combines functions into a new function.
Distractors are other paradigm terms, mainly from OOP.

items.prompt: What does `map(x => x * 2, [1, 2, 3])` produce?
rubric: map applies the function to every item and returns a new list.
12 confuses map with reduce.

items.prompt: Why are pure functions easier to test than impure ones?

options.label: They run faster, so a test suite finishes in less time overall
They are usually shorter, so fewer test cases are needed to cover them
Output depends only on inputs, so no outside state needs setup
They are type-checked by the compiler, so unit tests are not needed

rubric: Determinism removes hidden dependencies.
Distractors cite speed or length, which are not the reason.

items.prompt: What does `reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0, [1, 2, 3, 4])` return?
rubric: reduce folds the list into one value: the sum 10.
The list option confuses reduce with a running scan.

items.prompt: With immutable lists, what does adding an item to list `xs` typically do?

options.label: Deletes `xs` and rebuilds it silently
Changes `xs` in place and returns nothing at all
Raises an error every time
Creates a new list, leaving `xs` as is

rubric: Immutable updates yield new values.
In-place change is the mutable behaviour.

items.prompt: Which function is impure?

options.label: `f(x) = x * x`
`f(x) = x + counter++` using a global counter
`f(x, y) = x + y`
`f(s) = s.toUpperCase()` returning a new string

rubric: Changing and reading a global makes results vary and mutates state.
The others depend only on inputs.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain benefits of immutable data? Select all that apply.

options.label: It removes the need for any functions
It makes every program run faster
Values cannot change unexpectedly under other code
Sharing data between parts of a program is safer

rubric: Immutability prevents surprise changes and makes sharing safe.
Speed and removing functions are not guaranteed.

items.prompt: A function `makeAdder(n)` returns `x => x + n`. You run `const add5 = makeAdder(5)` and then call `add5(3)`. What is returned and why?

options.label: 8, because the inner function remembers n = 5
3, because n is gone after makeAdder finishes
An error, because n is out of scope
5, because the last argument replaces the first

rubric: The closure keeps n alive, so 3 + 5 = 8.
Distractors assume variables vanish after return.

items.prompt: Which function is pure?

options.label: `function f(x) { return x + Date.now(); }`
`function f(x) { n++; return x }`
`function f(x) { return x * 2; }`
`function f(x) { alert(x); return x; }`

rubric: It returns the same output for the same input and touches nothing outside itself.
Distractors hide a side effect (an alert, a counter) or non-determinism (the current time).

items.prompt: Why does immutable data make code more predictable?

options.label: Values never change after creation, so no other code can alter data you rely on
Immutable data forces functions to run one at a time, so timing never varies at all
The runtime encrypts immutable values, so other parts of the program cannot read them
Immutable data is stored in faster memory, so results always arrive in the same order

rubric: Without in-place changes, a value stays the same wherever it is shared.
Distractors invent performance, security or scheduling effects that immutability does not provide.

items.prompt: What does `map` do when given a function and a list?

options.label: Updates each element of the original list in place and returns nothing
Keeps only the elements for which the function returns true
Combines every element into a single value using the function
Builds a new list by applying the function to every element

rubric: map transforms each element and returns a new list of the same length.
Distractors describe filter, reduce, and an in-place loop.

items.prompt: Which of these is a higher-order function?

options.label: `function square(x) { return x * x; }`
`function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`
`function total(xs) { return xs.length * 2; }`
`function apply(f, x) { return f(x); }`

rubric: A higher-order function takes a function as an argument or returns one.
The others only work with plain values.

items.prompt: What does `[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0)` evaluate to?

options.label: `[false, true, false, true]`

rubric: filter keeps the elements for which the predicate is true, here the even numbers.
The boolean list confuses filter with map.

items.prompt: Which of these are side effects? Select all that apply.

options.label: Incrementing a global counter inside a function
Printing a message to the console
Adding two parameters and returning the sum
Building a new list from a list passed in

rubric: Changing outside state and doing I/O are observable effects beyond the return value.
Computing and returning new values from inputs is not a side effect.

items.prompt: A teammate writes `function addItem(cart, item) { cart.push(item); return cart; }`. After calling it, other code that still holds the old `cart` variable unexpectedly shows the new item too. In functional terms, what explains this?

options.label: The function is impure only because it returns a value instead of just printing it
`return cart` makes a hidden copy of the array, so older references become stale
Functions always receive a copy of the array, so earlier references are left stale
`push` changes the original array, so every variable pointing to it sees the item

rubric: push mutates the shared array in place, so all references observe the change.
Distractors wrongly assume copying happens automatically or misidentify what makes a function impure.

items.prompt: What does `[2, 3, 4].reduce((acc, n) => acc * n, 1)` return?
rubric: Starting at 1: 1*2*3*4 = 24.
9 sums instead of multiplying; 1 ignores the elements.

items.prompt: What does `[1, 3, 4].map(n => n * 2).filter(n => n > 5)` return?
rubric: map gives [2, 6, 8], then filter keeps values above 5: [6, 8].
Other options filter before doubling or mis-apply the threshold.

items.prompt: Given `const makeAdder = n => x => x + n; const add5 = makeAdder(5);`, what is `add5(3)`?
rubric: The closure remembers n = 5, so add5(3) = 3 + 5 = 8.
15 multiplies; 3 and 5 ignore one of the values.

items.prompt: Which expression returns a new array containing `newItem` while leaving `items` unchanged?

options.label: `items.splice(items.length, 0, newItem)`
`items[items.length] = newItem`
`items.push(newItem)`
`[...items, newItem]`

rubric: Spread copies the elements into a new array with the item appended.
The others all modify the original array in place.

items.prompt: Let `f = x => x + 1` and `g = x => x * 2`. With `compose(f, g)(x)` defined as `f(g(x))`, what is `compose(f, g)(5)`?
rubric: 12 applies f first, then g.

items.prompt: Given `const nums = [1, 2, 3];`, which expressions leave `nums` unchanged? Select all that apply.

options.label: `nums.filter(n => n > 1)`
`nums.push(4)`
`nums.reverse()`
`nums.map(n => n * 2)`

rubric: map and filter return new arrays.
reverse and push mutate the original array.

items.prompt: A shop has `orders = [{total: 40}, {total: 15}, {total: 25}]`. A developer runs `orders.filter(o => o.total > 20).map(o => o.total * 0.9).reduce((s, t) => s + t, 0)`. What value results?
rubric: Orders above 20 are 40 and 25; discounted they are 36 and 22.5; the sum is 58.5.
65 skips the discount; 72 discounts every order; 36 drops the second order.

items.prompt: Given `nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`, which pipeline returns the sum of the squares of the even numbers?

options.label: `reduce(add, filter(isEven, map(square, nums)), 0)` giving 91
`reduce(add, filter(isEven, nums), 0)` giving 12
`reduce(add, map(square, nums), 0)` giving 91
`reduce(add, map(square, filter(isEven, nums)), 0)` giving 56

rubric: Filtering evens first gives 2,4,6; squares 4,16,36 sum to 56.
Distractors skip filtering, filter squares incorrectly, or omit the squaring step.

items.prompt: Given `const add = a => b => a + b;` and `const inc = add(1);`, what does `[10, 20].map(inc)` return?

options.label: A function waiting for another argument

rubric: add(1) returns a closure with a=1, so each element gets 1 added.
Distractors confuse currying with summing the list or think map returns functions.

items.prompt: You must produce a new list from `xs = [3, 1, 2]` sorted ascending without changing `xs`. Which approach fits an immutable style?

options.label: Assign `ys = xs` and call `ys.sort()`
Sort a copy, such as `sorted(xs)`
Sort `xs` in place, then save a copy of the result
Call `xs.sort()` and return `xs`, since it sorts in place

rubric: Sorting a copy leaves the original unchanged.
Aliasing with `ys = xs` still mutates the same list, which learners often miss.

items.prompt: Using `compose(f, g)(x) = f(g(x))`, with `double = x => x * 2` and `inc = x => x + 1`, what does `compose(double, inc)(5)` return?
rubric: inc runs first: 6, then double: 12.
11 comes from reversing the order; the others misapply one function.

items.prompt: Which call computes the product of `[2, 3, 4]` with `reduce(fn, list, initial)`?

options.label: `reduce((acc, x) => acc * x, [2, 3, 4], 0)`
`reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, [2, 3, 4], 1)`
`reduce((acc, x) => acc * x, [2, 3, 4], 1)`

rubric: Multiplication needs identity 1 and a multiply step.
An initial 0 makes everything 0; addition or returning x gives wrong results.

items.prompt: Which of these functions are pure? Select all that apply.

options.label: `const f = (x) => x * 2`
`const f = (x) => x + Date.now() % 1`
`const f = (list) => { list.sort(); return list; }`
`const f = (list) => [...list].sort()`

rubric: Pure functions depend only on inputs and have no side effects.
Randomness and mutation of arguments break purity.

items.prompt: A shopping cart is `[{price: 10, qty: 2}, {price: 5, qty: 3}]`. You need the total cost without mutating the cart or using a loop with an accumulator variable. Which expression does this?

options.label: `cart.reduce((a, i) => a + i.price, 0)` giving 15
`cart.filter(i => i.qty > 2).length` giving 1
`cart.map(i => i.price * i.qty).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` giving 35
`cart.map(i => i.price + i.qty).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` giving 20

rubric: Line totals 20 and 15 sum to 35 with no mutation.
Distractors sum only prices or quantities, or count items.

items.prompt: A loop-created list of callbacks `fns` is built with `var i` in `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i)`. Calling each gives `3, 3, 3`. What is the cause?

options.label: Closures cannot capture loop variables, so they default to the final bound
All closures share one function-scoped `i`, which is 3 after the loop ends
The arrow functions are evaluated eagerly when pushed, using the last index
Each closure copies the value of `i` at creation, but the loop increments twice

rubric: Closures capture variables, not values; var is shared across iterations.
Distractors assume value-copy capture or eager evaluation.

items.prompt: `const total = items.map(i => { counter++; return i.price; })` is used, and `counter` is read later. Tests pass alone but fail when run in a different order. What is the underlying issue?

options.label: The map callback mutates shared state, so results depend on call history
map is lazy in JavaScript, so the callback may not have run when `counter` is read
map may run callbacks out of index order, so counter ends up with different values
A callback returning a number is treated as pure, so the counter update gets skipped

rubric: Mutating outer state makes the function impure and order-dependent.
Distractors blame laziness or nonexistent random ordering.

items.prompt: Two implementations compute `xs.filter(p).map(f)`. A: filter then map. B: map then filter using `f` result `y => p(y)`. They give different results for `xs=[1,2,3]`, `p = x => x > 1`, `f = x => x - 1`. Why?

options.label: A drops elements before mapping, which changes the list length of `f`
Both are equal; the difference comes from floating point rounding
B is always wrong because map must follow filter by language rule
Filter and map do not commute when `f` changes the values that `p` tests

rubric: A gives [1,2]; B maps to [0,1,2] then keeps >1, giving [2]. Order matters when f alters tested values.
Distractors invent rules or blame rounding.

items.prompt: A `reduce` that builds an object uses `(acc, x) => { acc[x.id] = x; return acc; }` with initial value a shared constant `EMPTY = {}`. Second call returns stale entries. What is the diagnosis?

options.label: reduce caches results between calls by default
The accumulator is the shared `EMPTY` object, mutated across calls
The id keys are strings, so entries are duplicated
The callback returns acc, which makes reduce skip resetting it

rubric: Mutating a shared initial value leaks state between calls.
Distractors invent caching or key-type problems.

items.prompt: A function `memoize(f)` caches results by argument. It gives wrong answers for `getPrice(id)`, which reads a database that changes. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: Memoization breaks because `id` is a primitive number, and caches can only key on object references
Memoization only pays off for recursive functions like Fibonacci, so it gives wrong results elsewhere
The cache should hold the functions themselves rather than values, since values are always stale
It assumes referential transparency, but `getPrice` is impure, so cached values go stale

rubric: Caching is safe only when output depends solely on inputs.
Distractors misstate where memoization applies.

items.prompt: A function `addItem(cart, item)` does `cart.items.push(item); return cart;`. Callers keep an earlier `cart` for undo and it changes unexpectedly. Which statements correctly analyse this? Select all that apply.

options.label: The earlier reference and returned value are the same object, so undo history is altered
Returning `cart` makes the function pure because it has a return value
A shallow copy `{...cart}` alone would still share the `items` array, so push would still mutate it
Wrapping the call in `Object.freeze(cart)` would make `push` on `cart.items` throw, so the old cart stays unchanged

items.prompt: A team replaces a loop with `data.map(parse).filter(valid).map(format)` on a list of 5 million records and sees memory spikes. Each stage builds a full intermediate array. Which analysis best explains the spike and a fitting remedy?

options.label: map and filter mutate the source array in place, so copies pile up as it grows; switch to a for loop that avoids copies
Chaining creates a new closure per record that is never freed, so memory climbs; avoid composition and call each function directly
The functions are impure, so the runtime caches every result it computes; wrap each step in memoization to cut the cost
Eager stages allocate intermediate arrays; fuse steps or use lazy iterators

rubric: Eager chained operations allocate intermediate collections; laziness or fusion avoids it.
Distractors misattribute the cost to mutation, impurity or closures.

items.prompt: A team parallelises `xs.reduce((a, b) => a - b)` by splitting the list into chunks, reducing each chunk, then combining the partial results in order. Results differ from the sequential run. What is the root cause?

options.label: Subtraction is not commutative, so the chunk results end up combined in the wrong order
Subtraction is not associative, so regrouping the operations into chunks changes the result
Each chunk's reduce starts without the previous chunk's running total, so partial results are off by one element
Reduce needs a numeric accumulator type, and chunked partial results are no longer plain numbers

rubric: Combining chunk results requires an associative operation; (a-b)-c differs from a-(b-c).
Commutativity is a tempting distractor, but order is preserved here, so it is not the issue.

items.prompt: A generic `memoize(f)` caches results under the key `args.join(',')`. It returns a wrong cached value for `f('a,b', 'c')` after `f('a', 'b,c')` was called, though `f` is pure. What is the flaw?

options.label: Memoization only works when `f` takes one argument, so the second call is ignored
Different argument lists can yield the same key string, so distinct calls collide
Pure functions cannot be safely memoized when any of their arguments are strings, because strings are compared by value
The cache is stored in a closure, so it is shared between different wrapped functions

rubric: The key function is not injective: both calls serialise to 'a,b,c'.
Purity of f is not the problem; the cache key design is.

items.prompt: In Python 3, a developer writes `results = map(log_and_double, items)` where `log_and_double` prints each item and returns double. Nothing is printed and no error occurs. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: `map` runs in a background thread, so the output appears only after the program exits
`map` returns a lazy iterator, so the function only runs when the results are consumed
`map` silently discards functions that have side effects, so `log_and_double` is skipped
`map` requires a list as its input, so the call quietly fails on other iterables

rubric: Python 3 map is lazy; evaluation happens on iteration.
Side effects inside map hide the timing problem, which is why they are discouraged.

items.prompt: A reducer does `const next = { ...state, count: state.count + 1 }` and later code calls `next.items.push(x)`. The previous state snapshot now also shows the new item. Why?

options.label: Spread freezes the properties it copies, so the push is applied to the original array in the old object
Spread copies only top-level properties, so `items` is the same array in both objects
`state.count + 1` mutates `state` in place, and that change then leaks into the `items` array
Objects created with spread stay linked to the original through the prototype chain, so changes show in both

rubric: Spread is a shallow copy; nested arrays remain shared references.
The prototype-chain idea confuses spread with Object.create.

items.prompt: With `const divide = curry((a, b) => a / b)`, a developer wants to halve every number and writes `map(divide(2), [4, 8])`, getting `[0.5, 0.25]`. What is the cause?

options.label: `divide(2)` fixes the numerator, so the argument order is wrong for a data-last pipeline
Curried functions evaluate lazily, so the values shown are not yet computed
Currying converts division to integer division, which reverses the results
`map` passes elements to the callback as the first argument, so the numbers are swapped

rubric: Partial application fixes leading parameters; here 2 became the dividend.
Fix by putting the data argument last, e.g. `divisor` first.

items.prompt: Which of these functions are impure, based on how they behave? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reads a reassignable module-level `rate` that other code can change
Writes a line to the console and returns its input
Builds a local array with `push`, then returns it
Returns `Math.max(...nums)`

rubric: Reading mutable external state and performing I/O both break purity.
Local mutation that never escapes is unobservable, so (b) stays pure.

items.prompt: A service indexes 100,000 records with `records.reduce((acc, r) => ({ ...acc, [r.id]: r }), {})`. Profiling shows run time grows roughly quadratically with record count, and memory churn is high. Other `reduce` calls over the same data that return numbers run fast. What best explains the slowdown?

options.label: `reduce` is inherently slower than loops because every step allocates a closure
Each step copies the whole accumulator, so total work is the sum of 1..n copies
Spread performs a deep clone of each record, so the cost scales with record size
Computed property keys force the engine to re-hash the entire object on every read

rubric: Copying an accumulator of size k at each of n steps gives O(n^2) work.
Numeric reductions do not copy a growing structure, which is why they stay fast.

items.prompt: A hot function must build a sorted, de-duplicated list from 1M items. Criteria: callers must never see their input modified, and throughput matters. Which design best meets both?

options.label: Use a local Set and array inside, then return a new array; the input is never touched
Deep-clone the input first and then mutate the clone freely at each step, so no caller can ever see a change
Sort and de-duplicate the caller's array in place and document it, since avoiding any copy is the fastest
Build a new immutable array for each operation, which guarantees purity even though memory use triples

rubric: Local, unobservable mutation keeps the interface pure while avoiding needless copies.
Deep cloning and per-step copies waste throughput; in-place mutation violates the stated caller guarantee.

items.prompt: An editor keeps a 50 MB document state and applies thousands of small edits per minute. Criteria: keep old versions for undo, and keep each update cheap. Which approach is best?

options.label: Use a persistent data structure with structural sharing so unchanged parts are reused
Freeze the state object and rebuild it from the original file after each edit
Mutate one state object in place and keep a log of inverse operations to replay for undo
Deep clone the full state on each edit so every snapshot is fully independent

rubric: Structural sharing gives cheap updates and retained snapshots.
Deep cloning meets undo but fails the cost criterion.

items.prompt: A colleague proposes making `saveUser` pure by having it return `Promise.resolve(db.insert(user))`. Judge this proposal.

options.label: It is flawed, because a Promise can only wrap asynchronous work, and a database insert is blocking so it cannot be deferred
It works, because a Promise is an immutable value once created, and returning an immutable value is all that purity requires
It works, because a Promise defers the insert until someone awaits it, so no side effect happens during the call itself
It is flawed, because the insert runs immediately on call; purity needs the effect described as a value and run later

rubric: The argument `db.insert(user)` is evaluated eagerly, so the effect has already happened.
A pure approach returns a description of the effect that an interpreter runs later.

items.prompt: A pipeline does `map`, `filter`, `map` over 10M rows on arrays, creating two large intermediates. Criteria: bounded memory, keep the declarative style, and avoid hand-written index loops. Which is the best choice?

options.label: Keep the eager array chain but move the filter first so every later step sees fewer rows
Cache each intermediate array on disk between steps so the chain code stays unchanged
Replace the chain with one `for` loop that mutates three counters and a result list
Compose the steps into one lazy iterator or transducer pass over the rows

rubric: Lazy or fused passes remove intermediates while staying declarative.
Hand loops give up the style criterion; disk caching adds cost without fixing the cause.

items.prompt: `isExpired(token)` calls `Date.now()` internally and its tests are flaky. Criteria: deterministic tests, no shared mutable test state, minimal ceremony. Which refactor is best?

options.label: Change it to `isExpired(token, now)` and have callers pass the current time
Create a singleton `Clock` whose time tests can set before each case
Patch the global `Date` in each test and restore it afterwards
Add a mutable `this.clock` field to the token class and swap it in tests

rubric: Passing time as an argument makes the function pure and trivially testable.
Global patches, singletons and mutable fields all keep shared mutable state.

items.prompt: A team is judging whether to use immutable updates for UI state. Which claims correctly justify the choice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Immutable updates eliminate allocation, so memory use always drops
Old snapshots can be retained for undo or time-travel debugging
Immutability prevents data races even when other code mutates shared globals
Change detection can use cheap reference equality, since a changed value is a new object

rubric: Reference equality checks and kept snapshots are real benefits of immutability.
Immutable updates usually allocate more, and they do not protect against unrelated shared mutable globals.

items.prompt: A signup form has independent field checks (email, age, username). Criteria: every error must be reported at once, checks must compose without try/catch, and callers must be forced to handle failure. A teammate suggests four designs. Which best meets all criteria?

options.label: Return `null` for invalid fields and let the UI skip any that are missing
Chain short-circuiting `Either` checks, so the first failure is returned and later checks are skipped
Throw an exception on the first invalid field and catch it once at the top level
Use a validation type that combines independent results and accumulates all errors in one value

rubric: An accumulating (applicative) validation type reports all errors and forces handling.
A short-circuiting Either reports only the first failure, which is the strongest distractor.

items.prompt: You will split a large list into chunks, reduce each chunk in parallel, then combine the partial results. Judged on getting the same answer as a sequential reduce, which combiner and identity pair is safe?

options.label: String concatenation, identity empty string
Integer subtraction, identity 0
Pairwise mean of two values, identity 0
Integer division, identity 1 per chunk, any order

rubric: Parallel chunked reduce needs an associative combiner with a true identity; concatenation has both.
Subtraction, mean and division are not associative, so regrouping chunks changes the result.

items.prompt: You want to memoize one function for speed without changing program behaviour. Judged on that criterion, which is the best candidate?

options.label: An ID generator that increments a shared counter and returns the new value
A price formatter that consults the current locale setting on every call
A route-cost function whose result depends only on its immutable arguments
A tax lookup that reads a rate from a config object other code may reassign later

rubric: Memoization is only behaviour-preserving when output depends solely on arguments.
The other options depend on mutable or changing state, so cached values would go stale or skip needed effects.

items.prompt: A store holds a 1,000,000-entry collection with frequent single-entry updates, and the app must keep earlier versions for undo. Judged on update time and memory, which approach is best?

options.label: Freeze the top-level object and mutate nested values, since a frozen top level keeps earlier versions safe from later changes
Use a persistent structure with structural sharing, so each update copies only the path to the changed entry
Deep copy the whole collection on every update, so each saved version is fully isolated from later updates
Mutate in place and record a reverse diff per update, so undo replays diffs instead of storing whole copies

rubric: Structural sharing gives cheap updates and keeps old versions valid by reusing unchanged nodes.
Deep copy is correct but wasteful; shallow freezing does not protect nested data.

items.prompt: A reviewer says: 'Any function that mutates an array is impure and must be rewritten.' The function `sortedCopy(xs)` copies `xs` into a new local array, sorts that array in place, and returns it. Which judgement is best?

options.label: The claim holds: in-place sorting is mutation, and purity forbids mutation anywhere in a function body
The claim fails only if the result is also memoized, because purity depends on caching behaviour
The claim holds: returning a mutated array means the output depends on hidden state in the sort
The claim fails: only a local copy is mutated and no caller can observe it, so the function stays pure

rubric: Purity is about observable behaviour: same inputs give the same output and no visible effects; encapsulated local mutation qualifies.
Distractors confuse purity with a ban on any mutation or with caching.

items.prompt: A pure but expensive function `f` must be applied to 10 million records, but you need only the first record where `f(record) > 100`. Judged on total work and clarity, which is best?

options.label: Map `f` over all records into a list, then filter, then take the first, so each stage is a separate, easily tested step
Build a lazy pipeline of map, filter and first so `f` stops running after the first match
Memoize `f` and map it eagerly over all records, so repeated inputs are served from the cache
Run the eager map in parallel across cores, so the wall-clock time falls with the core count

rubric: Lazy evaluation of a pure pipeline avoids wasted calls and keeps the stages readable.
Eager, memoized or parallel eager options still compute every record.

items.prompt: A team adopts 'functional core, imperative shell'. Which claims about this design are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: The program becomes faster, since pure functions are always cheaper to run than impure ones
Core logic can be tested by passing inputs and checking outputs, with no mocks for I/O
Side effects disappear entirely, because the shell is written in a functional style
Decisions stay in pure functions while the shell only performs the effects they describe

rubric: The pattern isolates effects at the boundary, making the core testable and decisions pure.
It does not remove effects or guarantee speed.

items.prompt: A reviewer flags `items.reduce((acc, x) => [...acc, transform(x)], [])` on 200,000 items as slow, because each step copies the accumulator, giving quadratic time. The team wants linear time and no mutation visible outside the function. Which resolution is best?

options.label: Push into an array declared outside the function inside a forEach, since that is linear and simple
Replace the reduce with a single map call, which is linear and mutates nothing the caller can see
Rewrite as recursion that spreads the head onto the recursive result, which restores linear time
Keep the spread, since immutability rules forbid mutating even a freshly created accumulator

rubric: A single map is linear and has no externally visible mutation.
Shared outer arrays leak mutation; recursion with spread is still quadratic and risks stack depth.

items.prompt: Design a three-step pipeline (parse, check range, normalise). Constraints: steps compose, expected failures do not use exceptions, and the pipeline stops at the first failure and reports its reason. Which design fits?

options.label: Each step sets a shared error flag, and every later step checks the flag before doing its own work
Each step returns a Result of value or error, chained with flatMap so later steps are skipped after a failure
Each step returns null on failure, and the caller checks for null between steps in a long chain of conditionals
Each step throws on failure and one outer try/catch logs the message, which keeps step signatures simple

rubric: A Result type chained with flatMap composes, avoids exceptions and carries the first error.
Null, exceptions and shared flags lose the reason, break composition or add hidden state.

items.prompt: You must implement `map(f, xs)` using only `reduce`, so that it returns a new list in the original order, does not mutate `xs`, and is safe to call on a large input. Which implementation best meets the first two requirements while remaining a pure function?

options.label: `xs.reduce((acc, x) => acc.push(f(x)), [])`
`xs.reduce((acc, x) => [f(x), ...acc], [])`
`xs.reduce((acc, x) => [...acc, f(x)], [])`
`xs.reduce((acc, x) => f(x), [])`

rubric: Appending to a fresh copy keeps order and avoids mutation.
The push version returns a number, prepending reverses the order, and the third discards the accumulator.

items.prompt: Constraint: compose `map(f)` and `filter(p)` once, then run them in a single pass over any collection type with no intermediate lists. Which building block meets this?

options.label: Transformers of reducers, such as `map(f) = rf => (acc, x) => rf(acc, f(x))`, composed by ordinary composition
Functions from list to list, such as `map(f) = xs => xs.map(f)`, composed so each stage builds its own list
A class wrapping a list that each stage mutates and then returns itself so calls can be chained
A recursive function that concatenates the mapped head onto the result computed from the tail

rubric: Reducer transformers compose into one reducer, giving a single pass independent of collection type.
The other options allocate intermediate collections or tie the design to lists and mutation.

items.prompt: A pure function `price(item, region)` is wrapped by a teammate's `memoize(fn)` that stores results in a Map keyed by the first argument only. What is the design missing?

options.label: A time-to-live on each entry, since results of a pure function expire after a while
A lock around the Map, since pure functions cannot be cached without mutual exclusion
A deep copy of every returned value, since caching a pure result would otherwise make it impure
A cache key built from every argument, so calls differing only in region do not collide

rubric: The key must capture all inputs that determine the output, otherwise different calls return wrong cached values.
The other options address non-issues for a pure function.

items.prompt: State is `{user: {profile: {name, tags}, prefs}, cart}`. You need `rename(s, name)` that returns new state with the name changed, leaves the original untouched, and reuses unchanged branches. Which implementation meets all of that?

options.label: `Object.assign(s, {user: {profile: {name}}})`
`{...s, user: {...s.user, name}}`
`{...s, user: {...s.user, profile: {...s.user.profile, name}}}`
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(s))`, then set the name on the clone

rubric: Copying only the objects along the path keeps the original intact and shares prefs, tags and cart.
The clone shares nothing, the second puts name in the wrong place, and the third mutates s and drops fields.

items.prompt: `applyDiscount(order)` reads `Date.now()`, mutates `order.total`, and writes an audit line to a file. Constraints: the same inputs always give the same output, and callers see no mutation. Which changes move toward that design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Pass the current date in as a parameter
Return a new order object with the updated total
Wrap the file write in try/catch so failures are handled
Cache the result of Date.now() in a module-level variable so repeated calls agree

items.prompt: An editing app must support undo, redo, and exact replay of a user session for bug reports. All state changes come from a stream of user actions. Which design meets all three requirements?

options.label: Model state as a fold of actions through a pure `reduce(state, action)`, keeping the action list and prior immutable states
Let each handler save a snapshot to disk before changing state, then restore the latest snapshot on undo
Keep one mutable state object updated by handlers, and log the method names called so they can be replayed later
Store only the current state and compute undo by running each handler's inverse using fresh timestamps

rubric: A pure reducer over recorded actions is deterministic, so replay is exact and undo/redo just move through retained states.
The others depend on mutable state, ad hoc snapshots or non-deterministic inverses.
